title: Signal Boost Rescue
covers: creating and checking equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both terms by the same number, instead of adding the same number to both terms
cert: finding, simplifying, and checking equivalent ratios

intro.caption: Lesson 3-9 — equivalent ratios. Zara's hover-kart stalled on the canyon loop! The emergency radio relay only boosts the signal when the pit crew sends an equivalent ratio.

balloons.t: Pit crew, my signal is fading! The relay needs a code equivalent to 2:5!
Hurry! My backup battery runs on pure sarcasm, and I'm running low!
Add 3 to both numbers of 2:5! That gives 5:8. Send it!
Wait, Beck! Adding 3 changes the ratio! Equivalent ratios MULTIPLY or DIVIDE both parts.

pages.caption: Adding the same number to both terms breaks a ratio. To make an equivalent ratio, multiply or divide both terms by the same number.

balloons.t: Multiply both parts of 2:5 by the same scale factor to boost the signal!
Zara's echo just came back as 18:24! Even my lunch has a simpler ratio!
Divide both 18 and 24 by the same number to simplify it back down.
The relay screen is flashing four candidate codes. Only the equivalent ones unlock!
Watch out for flipped orders and sneaky adding tricks!
Three final relay locks: scale up, simplify down, and solve a proportion!
Signal locked, power restored, and Zara glides home to loud cheers!

win.caption: Equivalent ratios represent the same comparison. Multiply or divide both terms by the same nonzero number—never add or subtract.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Multiply Both Terms
gates.prompt: Boost the base signal 2:5 by multiplying both terms by the same scale factor.
hints: Conceptual: multiplying both parts of a ratio by the same number keeps the relationship identical.
Procedural: if the first term is multiplied by 4, multiply the second term by 4 as well.

steps: Practice: scale 3:4 by a factor of 5.
worked.q: Scale 3:7 by a factor of 2. What is the second term?

items.label: 2:5 = 8:___ (missing second term)
items.aria: missing second term equivalent to 2 to 5 when first term is 8

fb.msg: 11 adds 6 to 5 (since 2 + 6 = 8). Equivalent ratios MULTIPLY both parts by 4, never add!
10 doubles 5, but 2 became 8 (× 4). Multiply 5 by 4 too.

items.fbDefault: Find what 2 was multiplied by to get 8 (× 4), then multiply 5 by that same factor.

options.fb: That added 3 to both terms (3+3=6, 4+3=7). Adding breaks the ratio.
4:3 flips the order of the two quantities.
Only the second term was doubled while the 3 stayed unchanged.

gates.pass: 8:20 locks in! The canyon tower lights up two bars stronger.

gates.title: Gate 2 · Simplify by Dividing
gates.prompt: Simplify Zara's echo signal by dividing both terms by the same common factor.
hints: Conceptual: dividing both terms by the same number makes smaller numbers that keep the exact same comparison.
Procedural: find the greatest common factor of both numbers and divide each part by it.

worked.q: Simplify 10:15. What is the first term?

items.label: Simplify 18:24 → 3:___
items.aria: simplified second term of 18 to 24 when first term is 3

fb.msg: That subtracted 15 from both numbers. Divide both 18 and 24 by 6.
24 ÷ 3 = 8, but 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so divide 24 by 6 as well.

items.q: Which simplified ratio is equivalent to 14:21?

options.fb: Only 14 was divided by 7. Divide both terms by 7.
That subtracted 7 from both terms instead of dividing both by 7.
The order got flipped. 14 ÷ 7 = 2 comes first, 21 ÷ 7 = 3 comes second.

gates.pass: 3:4 and 2:3! The static clears from Zara's helmet radio.

gates.title: Gate 3 · Check the Pairs
gates.prompt: Select every code on the relay screen that is equivalent to 2:5.
hints: Conceptual: check whether both parts of 2:5 were multiplied by the SAME number, and in the same order.
Procedural: test each option by dividing its first term by 2 and its second term by 5—do you get the same factor?

steps: Practice: check which of 6:9, 6:10, 4:6 is equivalent to 2:3.

options.fb: 4:7 added 2 to both terms of 2:5 instead of multiplying both by 2.
5:2 flips the order of the ratio.

items.fbMiss: Check every option: multiply both 2 and 5 by 2, 3, or 5.
items.fbExtra: Remove any ratio that added a number or flipped the order.

gates.pass: 4:10, 6:15, and 10:25 all chime green! The relay dish locks onto Zara's kart.

gates.title: Boss Gate · Full Signal Override
gates.prompt: Three final locks to beam full power to Zara's hover-kart.
hints: Conceptual: equivalent ratios always scale both terms by the same multiplier or divisor.
Procedural: find the scale factor between the two known numbers, then apply it to find the missing term.

items.label: Lock 1 · Scale up 3:5 = ___:35 (missing first term)
items.aria: missing first term in 3 to 5 equals blank to 35

fb.msg: 33 added 30 to both terms. Multiply 3 by the scale factor 7 (since 5 × 7 = 35).

items.fbDefault: Find the scale factor (35 ÷ 5 = 7), then multiply 3 by 7.

fb.msg: That subtracted 22 from both terms. Divide both 24 and 36 by 12.

items.q: Lock 3 · Beck says 6:8 and 9:11 are equivalent because "you add 3 to both." Is he right?

options.t: No — adding 3 changes the ratio; 6:8 simplifies to 3:4, and 9:11 does not
Yes — adding the same number always keeps ratios equivalent
options.fb: Adding the same number changes the comparison. Only multiplying or dividing both terms works.
The arithmetic is right, but adding does not preserve a ratio. 6:8 = 3:4, while 3:4 × 3 = 9:12.

gates.pass: BWOOOOM! Full power surges to Zara's hover-kart—she blasts out of the canyon!

journal.heading: Lesson 3-9 — what the signal rescue taught us
rows: Multiply BOTH terms of a ratio by the same nonzero number to make an equivalent ratio.
Divide BOTH terms by a common factor to write an equivalent ratio with smaller numbers.
2:5 and 5:2 are not equivalent—always keep the two quantities in the same order.
Never add or subtract the same number from both terms. 2:5 + 3 gives 5:8, which breaks the ratio.
journal.quote: "Adding 3 to both numbers doesn't boost the signal—it just sends static." — Lin

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 3-9 (Equivalent Ratios). Covers generating equivalent ratios by multiplying or dividing both terms by the same factor, simplifying ratios, and refuting the additive misconception.
standards: Use ratio and rate reasoning to find and verify equivalent ratios
